chapterTitle: Ch 13. Neural Networks as Distribution Transformers

concepts.title: Checkpoint
concepts.one_liner: A checkpoint is a record of the parameter vector at a specific iteration of training.
concepts.content: A checkpoint is a record of the parameters at some iteration of training. Specifically, if the iterates of the parameter vector are $\theta^0, \theta^1, \ldots, \theta^T$, then any $\theta^k$ can be recorded as a checkpoint. These records allow for the visualization of how a network transforms a training dataset, layer by layer, at different stages over the course of training.
concepts.motivation_md: Checkpoints allow researchers to save and analyze the state of a model at various points during the optimization process, enabling progress tracking and the visualization of how representations evolve over time.
concepts.recap_md: - A checkpoint captures the parameter vector $\theta^k$ at a specific training iteration $k$.

concepts.title: Dimensionality reduction

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

concepts.one_liner: Dimensionality reduction tools project high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional spaces, such as 2D, to enable visualization.
concepts.content:
Deep representations are typically high-dimensional, making them difficult to visualize directly. Dimensionality reduction tools project high-dimensional data to a lower dimensionality, for example 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. While these techniques provide a rough view of the network's internal state, they are essential for understanding how modern deep nets (like transformers with tens of thousands of dimensions) represent datasets.

(see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...)
concepts.motivation_md: Because humans cannot visualize data beyond three dimensions, dimensionality reduction is necessary to inspect the high-dimensional feature spaces and internal representations learned by deep neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Projects high-dimensional data into lower dimensions (usually 2D or 3D).

slots.motivation: Because humans cannot visualize data beyond three dimensions, dimensionality reduction is necessary to inspect the high-dimensional feature spaces and internal representations learned by deep neural networks.

concepts.title: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

concepts.one_liner: t-SNE is a dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize high-dimensional deep net embeddings in a 2D space.
concepts.content:
t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a specific dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset. It projects high-dimensional embeddings (which can be tens of thousands of dimensions) down to 2D. The projection aims to keep the distance between two datapoints in the 2D view roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. This allows for the visualization of how semantic classes are separated or disentangled within the network's representation.

(see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...)
concepts.motivation_md: t-SNE is particularly effective at preserving local structure, making it a popular choice for visualizing the clusters and semantic separations that emerge in deep learning feature spaces.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps high-dimensional embeddings down to a 2D plane.

concepts.title: Neural networks as distribution transformers

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: A deep net can be thought of as transforming an input data distribution into an output data distribution layer by layer through a sequence of embeddings.
concepts.content: A deep net transforms an input data distribution, $p_{\text {data }}$, into an output data distribution, $p_{\text {out}}$, layer by layer. Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data, and we can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. The goal of a binary softmax classifier, for example, is to move the datapoints around until all the class 0 points end up moved to $(1,0)$ on the output layer and all the class 1 points end up moved to $(0,1)$. (see figure: Mapping plot for a `linear`-`relu` stack.) Most loss functions can also be interpreted from this angle: they penalize the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective helps explain how complex networks achieve classification or regression by geometrically reshaping data distributions into separable or target-aligned configurations.
concepts.recap_md: - Views a deep network as a sequence of transformations on a data distribution. - Represents each layer's activations as a distinct embedding $p_{\ell}$. - Maps the input distribution $p_{\text{data}}$ toward a target output distribution $p_{\text{out}}$.

concepts.title: Goal of a binary softmax classifier

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: The goal of a binary softmax classifier is to move datapoints until class 0 points end up at $(1,0)$ and class 1 points end up at $(0,1)$.
concepts.content: An incoming data distribution can be reshaped layer by layer into a desired configuration. The goal of a binary softmax classifier, for example, is to move the datapoints around until all the class 0 points end up moved to $(1,0)$ on the output layer and all the class 1 points end up moved to $(0,1)$. This is because the one-hot code for the integer 0 is $[1,0]$ and the one-hot code for the integer 1 is $[0,1]$.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a geometric interpretation of classification as the process of moving data points to specific locations in the output space.
concepts.recap_md: - Aims to map class 0 points to the coordinate $(1,0)$. - Aims to map class 1 points to the coordinate $(0,1)$.

slots.motivation: It provides a geometric interpretation of classification as the process of moving data points to specific locations in the output space.
slots.key_passage: - Aims to map class 0 points to the coordinate $(1,0)$. - Aims to map class 1 points to the coordinate $(0,1)$.

concepts.title: Embedding

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data.
concepts.content: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data. We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution, $p_{\text {data }}$, into an output data distribution, $p_{\text {out}}$, through a sequence of these embeddings. We can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. Layer by layer, a deep net transforms $p_{\text {data }}$ into $p_{\texttt{1}}$ into $p_{\texttt{2}}$, and so on until finally transforming the data to the distribution $p_{\text {out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Embeddings allow the network to transform raw input into increasingly useful, high-level representations for the task at hand.
concepts.recap_md: - Defines an embedding as the representation of data at a specific network layer. - Treats layer activations as a distribution $p_{\ell}$ in a sequence of transformations.

slots.motivation: Embeddings allow the network to transform raw input into increasingly useful, high-level representations for the task at hand.
slots.key_passage: - Defines an embedding as the representation of data at a specific network layer. - Treats layer activations as a distribution $p_{\ell}$ in a sequence of transformations.

concepts.title: Loss function as distribution divergence

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Most loss functions can be interpreted as penalizing the divergence between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.
concepts.content: Most loss functions can be interpreted as penalizing the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ of a neural network and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$. This perspective treats the deep net as a transformer of the input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ into an output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ through intermediate layer embeddings $p_{\ell}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective links optimization objectives to information theory and the geometric transformation of data distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Interprets loss functions as measuring the divergence between $p_{\text{out}}$ and $p_{\text{target}}$. - Frames training as the process of aligning output and target distributions.

slots.motivation: This perspective links optimization objectives to information theory and the geometric transformation of data distributions.
slots.key_passage: - Interprets loss functions as measuring the divergence between $p_{\text{out}}$ and $p_{\text{target}}$. - Frames training as the process of aligning output and target distributions.
slots.example: Most loss functions can be interpreted as penalizing the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ of a neural network and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$. This perspective treats the deep net as a transformer of the input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ into an output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ through intermediate layer embeddings $p_{\ell}$.

concepts.title: Visualizing 2D-to-2D mappings

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Visualizing 2D-to-2D mappings provides insight into how neural net layers act to transform a Gaussian blob of data.
concepts.content: Visualizing two-dimensional (2D)-to-2D mappings extends to visualizing the $N$-dimensional (ND)-to-ND mappings performed by real deep nets. Already 2D-to-2D visualizations can give a lot of insight into the general case. In @fig-neural_nets_as_data_transformations-2D_mapping_diagrams, we show how three common neural net layers may act to transform a Gaussian blob of data centered at the origin. (see figure: 2D mapping diagrams for several neural layers. The `linear` layer mapping will shift, stretch, and rotate depending on its weights and biases.)
concepts.motivation_md: Since high-dimensional transformations are difficult to visualize, 2D mappings serve as a useful proxy for understanding the geometric effects of different layers.

concepts.title: Sparsity in high-dimensional ReLU networks

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: In high-dimensional ReLU networks, almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes, resulting in very sparse representational geometry.
concepts.content: The relu layer maps many points to the axes of the positive quadrant. In general, with relu-nets, a lot of data density will build up along these axes, because any point not in the positive quadrant snaps to an axis. This effect becomes exaggerated in real networks with high-dimensional embeddings. In particular, for a width-$N$ layer, the region that is strictly positive occupies only $\frac{1}{2^N}$ proportion of the embedding space, so almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes after a relu layer. The geometry of high-dimensional neural representations may become very sparse because of this, where most of the volume of representational space is not occupied by any datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Explains the geometric origin of sparsity in ReLU-based networks and how high dimensionality affects the occupancy of the representation space.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps non-positive inputs to axes, concentrating data density along them. - Results in extremely sparse representations in high dimensions where only $\frac{1}{2^N}$ of the space is positive.
